output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation reveals a multi-domain amnestic profile. Verbal learning and delayed recall are disproportionately impaired (RAVLT delayed recall 8th percentile; immediate recall 15th percentile), with reduced visual delayed recall (Rey Complex Figure delayed recall 12th percentile) and an intact copy (40th percentile). Confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 20th percentile) and semantic fluency (Category Fluency Animals, 18th percentile) are mildly impaired. Set-shifting is borderline (Trail Making B, 22nd percentile); basic processing speed is intact (Trail Making A, 35th percentile). Screening: MoCA 22/30, MMSE 26/30. Geriatric Depression Scale 6/15 (borderline). The profile is consistent with amnestic multi-domain mild cognitive impairment.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 26/30 with impaired delayed recall partly helped by cues, informant-confirmed decline over twelve months, and preserved instrumental independence (billing errors isolated and compensated), staging the syndrome as mild cognitive impairment
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: A validated bedside instrument, the effect of cueing and the informant's account of daily function decide whether this man has mild cognitive impairment or dementia [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amnestic multi-domain profile: disproportionate verbal and visual delayed recall impairment with milder naming, semantic fluency and set-shifting deficits
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
action_criteria.rationale: The MMSE of 26/30 is insensitive in a highly educated man, so formal testing is needed to show the amnestic profile and the second domain, and gives a baseline for follow-up [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TSH, folate, syphilis and HIV serology normal; B12 305 pg/mL low-normal; HbA1c 7.3% above target
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid disease, B12 deficiency (he has taken metformin for 12 years), syphilis and metabolic factors must be excluded or addressed before the decline is attributed to neurodegeneration [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Methylmalonic acid 0.17 umol/L, normal: no functional deficiency
action_criteria.label: Measure methylmalonic acid to resolve the low-normal vitamin B12
action_criteria.rationale: A serum B12 of 305 pg/mL is indeterminate in a man on long-term metformin with reduced vibration sense at the toes; a normal methylmalonic acid excludes functional deficiency [BSH_B12_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild bilateral hippocampal atrophy (MTA 1-2) with subtle temporoparietal volume loss, Fazekas 2 white matter disease with a caudate lacune, and lobar parietal microbleeds
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
action_criteria.rationale: MRI shows the medial temporal atrophy that supports a neurodegenerative cause, quantifies the small vessel disease expected from his diabetes and hypertension, and excludes a mass, hydrocephalus or another structural cause [NIA_AA_2011] [STRIVE_2013].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity without established tau pathology: borderline decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio (0.060) with p-tau181 and total tau within range, or a positive amyloid PET in the low positive range
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine as routine treatment for mild cognitive impairment; neither is approved for MCI and the guideline does not support routine use [AAN_dementia_2018].

Do not add an antimuscarinic bladder drug (e.g. oxybutynin) for prostatic symptoms; anticholinergic burden worsens cognition, and tamsulosin, an alpha-1 blocker without anticholinergic effect, can continue [Beers_2023].
Do not attribute the decline to obstructive sleep apnea, low mood or normal aging alone; the amnestic multi-domain profile with hippocampal atrophy needs follow-up as mild cognitive impairment.
required_recommendations: Disclose amnestic multidomain mild cognitive impairment with suspected Alzheimer disease pathology and a vascular contribution to the patient and his wife, explaining that it is not dementia, the risk of progression, and the value of advance planning while he has full capacity [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].

Arrange cognitive and functional reassessment in 6 to 12 months and recommend regular exercise (at least twice weekly); explain that no medicine is approved for mild cognitive impairment [AAN_dementia_2018].

Manage vascular risk factors that contribute to his small vessel disease: glycaemic control (HbA1c 7.3%), blood pressure (135/77 mmHg), continued statin therapy, and regular CPAP use for obstructive sleep apnea [AAN_dementia_2018].

Review safety with the patient and his wife: driving (hesitation at complex intersections, disorientation in a car park) with a formal driving assessment if concerns grow, and a plan for oversight of finances if billing errors recur [AAN_dementia_2018].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

accepted: Amnestic multidomain mild cognitive impairment, suspected Alzheimer disease pathology (intermediate likelihood) with vascular contribution
mild cognitive impairment due to alzheimer

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / vascular contribution to dementia
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 small vessel disease, a caudate lacune, diabetes and hypertension make a vascular contribution likely, and it is part of the diagnosis; the gradual amnestic-predominant course with hippocampal atrophy, and a decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio when tested, argue against pure vascular cognitive impairment
No visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism, no REM sleep behavior disorder, no cognitive fluctuations described
No early personality change, disinhibition, or executive-predominant profile; memory is the dominant deficit, atypical for bvFTD

GDS 6/15 is borderline and he has withdrawn socially, but he denies depressed mood, and an insidious amnestic decline with impaired delayed recall on formal testing is not typical of depression-related cognitive impairment

differential.diagnosis: Reversible cognitive impairment from thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, or untreated sleep apnea
differential.key_features: TSH 2.6 mIU/L, folate normal, B12 305 pg/mL with normal methylmalonic acid (0.17 umol/L) and homocysteine (10.2 umol/L); intermittently treated mild OSA may add to morning fogginess but does not explain a progressive amnestic multi-domain decline

key_clinical_evidence: MMSE may remain within the 'normal' range in highly educated patients with early AD; MoCA and formal neuropsychological testing are more sensitive at the MCI / mild dementia interface

Mixed vascular and neurodegenerative pathology is common in older adults; small vessel disease does not exclude Alzheimer pathology, and lobar microbleeds raise cerebral amyloid angiopathy, which matters if anti-amyloid treatment is ever considered [Boston_CAA_2022].
A low-normal B12 in a patient on long-term metformin is indeterminate and should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before B12 deficiency is dismissed as a contributor [BSH_B12_2014].

Cholinesterase inhibitors are not approved for mild cognitive impairment and are not recommended routinely at this stage; serial assessment and vascular risk management are the evidence-based steps [AAN_dementia_2018].

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Vascular disease contributes to the picture, but a gradually progressive amnestic multi-domain profile with hippocampal atrophy points to suspected Alzheimer pathology as the main driver of a mixed presentation
red_herrings.data_point: Chronic lacunar infarct in the left caudate head plus Fazekas grade 2 small-vessel disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on pure vascular cognitive impairment and skip Alzheimer biomarker workup

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: OSA may contribute, but a progressive amnestic-predominant decline with hippocampal atrophy cannot be explained by OSA alone
red_herrings.data_point: Inconsistent CPAP use for obstructive sleep apnea
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute cognitive symptoms entirely to under-treated OSA and defer further neurodegenerative workup

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MMSE is insensitive for early AD especially in highly educated patients; MoCA 22/30 with disproportionate delayed-recall impairment is the more reliable finding
red_herrings.intended_effect: Reassure the agent that cognition is intact and stop the workup

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect, particularly in older patients
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.

findings.result: Alert and oriented to person, place, and year, but initially states the date as two days prior.
MMSE 26/30, losing points on delayed recall (1/3 at 5 minutes, improving to 2/3 with categorical cues), and one point lost on serial sevens.

Clock drawing shows correct number placement but the minute hand points to the 10 rather than the 2 when asked to set the time to '10 past 11'. Naming intact for common objects, with mild hesitation on lower-frequency items.

His wife reports a gradual decline over twelve months: misplacing objects, repeating questions, word-finding pauses, and two unpaid utility bills and a duplicate payment in the past six months. He now uses automatic payments and his phone and still manages the accounts and drives familiar routes himself.

clinical_assessment.impression: MMSE 26/30, with impairment in delayed recall, orientation to date and serial subtraction, and a stimulus-bound error on clock setting. Free recall 1/3 at 5 minutes, 2/3 with categorical cues: cueing helped partially. Category fluency 13 and letter fluency 10 in 60 seconds, low-normal. His wife reports decline over twelve months in memory, word finding and bill payment. The billing errors were isolated and are now compensated by his own strategies; instrumental independence is preserved, consistent with mild cognitive impairment rather than dementia.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, validated neuropsychological testing, the cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI; methylmalonic acid recommended for the low-normal B12. Amyloid status optional, by CSF or amyloid PET (one conclusive test).
key_educational_points: MMSE can appear falsely reassuring in highly educated patients; MoCA is more sensitive for detecting early impairment
Cerebrovascular disease commonly coexists with Alzheimer pathology in older adults, creating diagnostic complexity
Vascular risk factor optimization is critical in patients with mixed neurodegenerative and vascular pathology
Low-normal B12 should prompt functional testing (methylmalonic acid) before being dismissed
Sleep apnea with poor CPAP compliance is a modifiable contributor to cognitive impairment that should be addressed
Amyloid status can be established by CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET; one conclusive test is enough, and a borderline CSF result supports only an intermediate likelihood of MCI due to Alzheimer disease

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Eduardo Reyes is a 68-year-old right-handed retired civil engineer who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife, Carmen, for evaluation of subjective memory complaints that have been gradually worsening over the past twelve months. His wife first noticed the changes approximately a year ago when he began occasionally misplacing his reading glasses and wallet, which she initially attributed to normal absentmindedness. Over the ensuing months, however, she has observed that he sometimes struggles to find the right word during conversations, pausing mid-sentence and substituting a less specific word such as saying 'the thing' instead of naming the object he intends. He has also become somewhat repetitive, asking the same question two or three times within an hour without apparent awareness that he has already asked. His wife notes that he has always been meticulous about the household finances, but over the past six months she discovered two unpaid utility bills and a duplicate payment to their cable company. When she brought this to his attention, he became frustrated and defensive, insisting he had taken care of everything. He has since set up automatic payments for the recurring bills and still manages the household accounts himself, with no further errors in the last three months; his wife has not had to take over. He continues to drive on familiar routes without incident, though his wife has noticed he seems more hesitant at complex intersections. He recently got momentarily confused in a large parking garage at the mall and had to use his phone to locate their car. He remains independent in all activities of daily living including bathing, dressing, and grooming. His appetite is unchanged and sleep is described as fair, though he uses his CPAP inconsistently. He has been less enthusiastic about his woodworking hobby and has mentioned feeling 'foggy' some mornings. He denies visual hallucinations, personality changes, or aggressive behavior. There have been no episodes of getting lost while driving on well-known routes, no difficulty operating household appliances, and no falls. His wife denies witnessing any acting out of dreams or any limb jerking during sleep. He has not experienced headaches, seizures, tremor, or urinary incontinence. He has been somewhat more withdrawn socially in recent months but denies feeling depressed. He agreed to come to the appointment at his wife's insistence, acknowledging that 'things aren't as sharp as they used to be.'
